title: Making the invisible visible: how AI is transforming patient understanding of dental radiographs
html:
From identifying early bone loss to supporting more meaningful conversations about oral health, AI visualisation of dental radiographs is helping Gensmile’s dental professionals bridge the gap between clinical findings and patient understanding. 

For dental professionals, interpreting radiographs is an essential part of everyday clinical practice, but for patients, the subtle variations in grey which reveal important information about their teeth and supporting structures can be difficult to understand.

Explaining what a radiograph shows, why a particular finding matters and how it might influence future treatment can therefore present a significant communication challenge. This underpins the value AI-powered technology such as Pearl’s Second Opinion is offering clinicians to make these conversations more accessible, using colour-coded visualisations and annotations to help patients better understand what they are seeing.

Bringing radiographs to life

Gensmile has been implementing Pearl across its specialist and general practices. For specialist prosthodontist Josh Sharpling, one of the greatest opportunities lies in making complex clinical information easier to communicate.

As he says: ‘It’s just different shades of grey when you’re looking at a radiograph, and to be able to put colours onto it to tell the story of what the patient’s current situation is, it’s just so much easier to get that information across and to develop a narrative when it’s easier to see.’

By introducing colour and visual labels, AI-assisted radiograph analysis can help clinicians explain anatomical structures and draw attention to areas that warrant discussion.

This is particularly valuable when patients have little understanding of dental anatomy or what the different structures on an X-ray represent. As Josh explains, patients may struggle to distinguish between the tooth itself and the bone supporting it. While clinicians can describe these structures verbally, visual annotations offer a more immediate way to communicate the information.

The ability to compare annotated radiographs with previous X-rays can also help patients appreciate changes over time, making discussions about their oral health more tangible. Importantly, the aim is not simply to show patients what the clinician has identified, but to help them recognise and understand those findings for themselves.

Supporting periodontal conversations

The potential value of enhanced radiograph visualisation is particularly apparent in periodontal care, where understanding changes in bone support is an important part of patient education.

Gensmile’s clinical director Asad Rahman highlights the importance of clearly communicating the condition of the structures supporting the teeth: ‘What we’re looking at in terms of the support structures is really important. So, looking at the bone levels is really important.’

By using colour to distinguish the tooth, root and surrounding bone, AI-assisted visualisation can make these anatomical relationships easier for patients to interpret.

For Asad, one of the most significant opportunities is in discussions around early bone loss. He says: ‘The major significant change in periodontal management is looking at early bone loss, and I think that’s a really important tool.’

Where patients might previously have struggled to understand a verbal explanation of changes in bone levels, annotated radiographs can provide a visual starting point for the conversation.

A line indicating the relevant bone level, for example, can help clinicians highlight an area of concern without having to draw the annotation manually. This can support more focused discussions about periodontal health, helping patients engage with clinical findings and understand why ongoing monitoring or management may be necessary. Rather than replacing the clinician’s explanation, the technology provides a visual reference around which that explanation can be built.

Strengthening co-diagnosis

The use of visual information to support patient involvement is already well established in many dental practices. Clinical photography and intraoral scanning have become valuable communication tools because they allow patients to see familiar images of their own teeth.

Radiographs, however, have traditionally been less intuitive. Josh sees AI-enhanced radiographs as a natural extension of this visual approach to patient education: ‘Co-diagnosis is a big part of what we do already, using photographs and discussing things with patients. So I see this as a tool where I can build a story around what the patient’s current situation is.’

However, he notes that photographs and intraoral scans are relatively easy for patients to interpret because they resemble what patients see in the mirror. Adding colour and annotations to radiographs offers an opportunity to bring a similar level of accessibility to information that would otherwise remain difficult for patients to interpret. This approach can help create a more collaborative consultation, in which patients are better equipped to follow the clinician’s explanation, ask informed questions and participate in discussions about their care.

AI as a second opinion, not a replacement

While AI offers new opportunities to support clinical communication, its role within the diagnostic process must remain clearly defined. Sophie Lovett emphasises that Pearl’s Second Opinion is designed to support, rather than replace, professional clinical judgement: ‘It’s really important to know that Pearl’s Second Opinion is just that; it’s a second opinion. You, as the clinicians, are the first and primary decision makers.’

This distinction is fundamental to the responsible use of AI in dentistry. AI-generated annotations can provide an additional visual perspective and help draw attention to potential findings, but clinical interpretation, diagnosis and treatment decisions remain the responsibility of the dental professional. The value of the technology lies in its ability to complement clinical expertise while helping practitioners communicate their assessments more effectively.

A clearer picture for patients

As dentistry continues to embrace digital technologies, the opportunity to improve patient understanding is becoming an increasingly important consideration. AI-assisted radiograph visualisation offers a way to make traditionally complex images more accessible, particularly when discussing periodontal health, bone support and changes over time.

For clinicians already using photography and intraoral scans to involve patients in their care, annotated radiographs represent another useful addition to the communication toolkit.

Ultimately, the opportunity is not simply to introduce more technology into the consultation, but to use that technology to make clinical information easier to understand. By helping patients see what their dental professionals see, AI-powered visualisation has the potential to support clearer explanations, more meaningful conversations and a more collaborative approach to oral healthcare.
